triage.name: IgA nephropathy
triage.reason: Episodic gross hematuria after upper respiratory infection in a young adult; classic nephrology case with biopsy-based diagnosis and several glomerulonephritis look-alikes.

demographics: More common in males than females (roughly 2:1)
Highest incidence in the second and third decades of life
More common in East Asian and Caucasian populations than in African ancestry populations
A leading cause of primary glomerulonephritis worldwide

risk_factors.text: Family history of IgA nephropathy or another glomerulonephritis

family_history: IgA nephropathy in a first-degree relative
Other glomerulonephritis in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: My urine turned dark and cola-colored
I noticed blood in my urine
My urine looks like tea after I get a cold
My ankles are puffy in the morning

hpi.onset: Episodic; gross hematuria often appears within 1–3 days of a cold, sore throat or stomach bug, or it may be found on a routine urine test with no symptoms
hpi.duration: Each episode of visible blood lasts a few days; the underlying condition is chronic and lifelong
hpi.progression: Episodes of dark urine may recur with later infections; between episodes urine may look normal. Over years, some patients develop rising blood pressure, protein in the urine and slowly worsening kidney function
hpi.location: Kidneys; blood is seen in the urine, and swelling is usually in the ankles, feet and around the eyes
hpi.quality: Urine is smoky, tea- or cola-colored rather than bright red; swelling is soft and pitting
hpi.severity: Often mild to moderate; visible blood is alarming but usually not painful
hpi.timing: Blood appears with or shortly after an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection and clears over several days
relieving: Nothing specific; episodes resolve on their own

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the ankles or around the eyes
Flank or loin pain during an episode

pertinent_negatives: Recent sore throat with a positive strep test
Family history of kidney failure at a young age

negatives: Flank pain radiating to the groin

atypical.how_it_differs: Children more often present with a sudden episode of visible blood in the urine after a cold, and the urine can look bright red rather than cola-colored. They are less likely to have high blood pressure or swelling.
Older adults are more likely to be found on routine urine testing with blood and protein but no visible blood, and they may already have reduced kidney function or high blood pressure at diagnosis.
Blood and protein in the urine may be attributed to preeclampsia or a urinary infection; IgA nephropathy can also flare during pregnancy with worsening blood pressure and protein in the urine.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal link to a cold

atypical.how_it_differs: Patients with advanced kidney disease present with tiredness, poor appetite, nausea, itching and swelling rather than episodes of dark urine.

general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, may have periorbital or ankle puffiness
general.severe: Ill-appearing with marked edema, may be dyspneic if volume overloaded

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and around the eyes
findings.finding: Periorbital puffiness, worse in the morning

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of the foot or the medial malleolus for several seconds
findings.finding: Soft pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff

findings.finding: Costovertebral angle tenderness during an episode

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of the legs, buttocks and trunk
Inspect and palpate the small joints of the hands, wrists, knees and ankles
findings.finding: No joint swelling, warmth or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and oropharynx
findings.finding: No oral ulcers or mucosal lesions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck with the patient at 45 degrees and assess the internal jugular venous pulsation
Auscultate the heart at the apex with the bell

labs.caveat: Hematuria is the hallmark; it may be microscopic between episodes of gross hematuria. Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts on microscopy support a glomerular source.
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts point to a glomerular bleed rather than a lower urinary tract source.
Proteinuria is often absent early and may be intermittent; quantify with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio when present.
Red cell casts are highly specific for glomerulonephritis but are not always seen.
Many patients have normal kidney function at presentation; a rising creatinine indicates progressive disease.
Low albumin suggests significant protein loss and a nephrotic-range picture.
Anemia of chronic kidney disease in advanced disease.
Nonspecific; marked elevation should raise suspicion for a systemic vasculitis or lupus.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before biopsy or immunosuppressive therapy; also helps distinguish preeclampsia.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line to exclude obstruction or structural disease and to assess kidney size

findings.text: Normal-sized or slightly enlarged kidneys with increased echogenicity
Small, shrunken kidneys with cortical thinning in advanced chronic disease

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Usually normal; may show nonspecific renal enlargement

initial.why: Detects hematuria, proteinuria and red cell casts; first step in any suspected glomerulonephritis
Baseline hemoglobin and white count; anemia suggests chronic kidney disease
Rules out pregnancy before biopsy or immunosuppression
Excludes obstruction, stones and structural causes of hematuria

confirmatory.test: Kidney biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis; shows mesangial IgA deposits and defines the Oxford MEST-C score

supporting.why: Quantifies proteinuria, a key prognostic marker and treatment target
Assesses protein loss and nutritional status
Nonspecific inflammation; marked elevation suggests vasculitis or lupus
Nonspecific inflammation; helps screen for systemic disease
Normal in IgA nephropathy; low levels suggest lupus nephritis or post-infectious glomerulonephritis

supporting.only_if: systemic features such as rash, arthritis or cytopenias are present
pulmonary or systemic features are present

supporting.test: Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
supporting.why: Screens for monoclonal gammopathy in older adults with kidney disease
supporting.only_if: age over 50 or unexplained renal failure

supporting.test: Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody and HIV test
Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer and throat culture
supporting.only_if: recent sore throat and low complement

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for glomerular disease; contrast risks kidney injury
not_indicated.only_if: obstruction or mass suspected and ultrasound nondiagnostic

not_indicated.why: No role in hematuria or glomerulonephritis
Not indicated unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
No role in an afebrile, stable patient
Not part of the initial glomerulonephritis workup
Not needed unless diabetes is suspected as the cause of kidney disease

decision_points: Confirm a glomerular source of bleeding (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria) before pursuing biopsy
Exclude pregnancy before kidney biopsy or immunosuppressive therapy
Kidney biopsy is indicated for suspected IgA nephropathy with proteinuria, rising creatinine or atypical features
Normal complement levels favor IgA nephropathy over lupus or post-infectious glomerulonephritis
Rapidly progressive kidney failure with crescents may require immunosuppression rather than observation

criteria.name: Kidney biopsy diagnosis of IgA nephropathy
criteria.summary: Definitive diagnosis requires kidney biopsy showing dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, with mesangial proliferation on light microscopy and mesangial electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy. Secondary causes such as cirrhosis, celiac disease and HIV should be excluded.
items: Mesangial IgA deposits dominant or codominant on immunofluorescence
Mesangial electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy
No clinical or serologic evidence of systemic lupus erythematosus or vasculitis

criteria.name: Oxford MEST-C classification
criteria.summary: A pathology scoring system used to predict prognosis in IgA nephropathy based on biopsy features: mesangial hypercellularity (M), endocapillary hypercellularity (E), segmental glomerulosclerosis (S), tubular atrophy/interstitial fibrosis (T) and crescents (C).
items: T: tubular atrophy or interstitial fibrosis

differential.name: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
differential.why_considered: Same IgA-mediated small-vessel process with kidney involvement, hematuria and proteinuria, often after an upper respiratory infection
differential.trigger: Palpable purpura on the legs or buttocks, abdominal pain, or joint pain alongside the hematuria

history: Palpable rash on the legs and buttocks
Colicky abdominal pain or gastrointestinal bleeding
labs: Normal platelet count and coagulation studies
Hematuria and proteinuria similar to IgA nephropathy
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound may show bowel wall thickening or intussusception in children

differential.name: Post-infectious (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis
differential.why_considered: Hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and edema after an infection, the classic alternative to IgA nephropathy
differential.trigger: Dark urine 1–3 weeks after a sore throat or skin infection, with low complement levels

history: Sore throat or impetigo 1–3 weeks before the dark urine
No prior episodes of hematuria with colds
labs: Positive antistreptolysin O titer or positive throat culture
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show enlarged echogenic kidneys

differential.name: Lupus nephritis
differential.why_considered: Glomerular hematuria and proteinuria in a young patient, especially a woman, with systemic features
differential.trigger: Rash, oral ulcers, joint pain, cytopenias or low complement levels with the urine findings

history: Recurrent fevers, weight loss or night sweats
imaging: Kidney biopsy shows a full-house immunofluorescence pattern with IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q

differential.name: Alport syndrome
differential.why_considered: Hereditary glomerular hematuria, often presenting in young people with blood in the urine

history: Family history of kidney failure at a young age
Persistent microscopic hematuria rather than episodic gross hematuria after colds
exam: Ocular findings such as anterior lenticonus
imaging: Kidney biopsy shows thinning and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy

differential.name: Thin basement membrane disease
differential.why_considered: Benign familial microscopic hematuria that can be confused with early IgA nephropathy

history: Family history of hematuria without kidney failure
No episodes of gross hematuria after infections
imaging: Kidney biopsy shows a diffusely thin glomerular basement membrane without IgA deposits

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Blood in the urine and urinary symptoms

labs: Positive urine leukocyte esterase and nitrites
Bacteria and white cells on urine microscopy

differential.name: Nephrolithiasis
differential.why_considered: Blood in the urine with flank pain

history: Severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
labs: Hematuria without proteinuria or red cell casts
imaging: Stone and hydronephrosis on CT or ultrasound

severity.mild: Normal kidney function, isolated microscopic or episodic gross hematuria, minimal proteinuria, normal blood pressure
severity.moderate: Persistent proteinuria (often 1–3 g/day), hypertension, slowly rising creatinine but preserved kidney function
severity.severe: Proteinuria over 3 g/day, declining kidney function, or crescentic disease on biopsy with rapid loss of function
severity.critical: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with acute kidney injury, oliguria, fluid overload or need for dialysis

red_flags.finding: Rapidly rising creatinine over days to weeks
red_flags.meaning: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents; needs urgent biopsy and immunosuppression
High risk of progressive kidney failure and cardiovascular complications

red_flags.finding: Severe hypertension with headache, visual changes or seizures
red_flags.meaning: Hypertensive emergency; risk of encephalopathy and stroke
Acute kidney injury requiring urgent nephrology evaluation and possible dialysis

red_flags.finding: Macroscopic hematuria with clots or severe flank pain
red_flags.meaning: May indicate a coexisting stone or obstruction rather than glomerular bleeding alone

complications.name: Progressive chronic kidney disease
clues: Rising creatinine over months to years

complications.name: End-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplant
Acute kidney injury with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

special_populations.differences: More often present with sudden gross hematuria after a cold; blood pressure and kidney function are usually normal, and the long-term course is often milder than in adults.

More likely to be found on routine urine testing with microscopic hematuria and proteinuria; kidney function may already be reduced at diagnosis, and secondary causes such as cirrhosis or monoclonal gammopathy should be considered.

Hematuria and proteinuria may be mistaken for preeclampsia or a urinary infection; IgA nephropathy can flare during pregnancy with worsening blood pressure and proteinuria, requiring close monitoring.

Patients with advanced kidney disease present with fatigue, poor appetite, nausea, itching and edema rather than episodes of dark urine; management focuses on slowing progression and preparing for kidney replacement therapy.

key_questions.question: What does your urine look like, and when did you first notice it?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoky, tea- or cola-colored urine rather than bright red; onset within 1–3 days of a cold or stomach bug

key_questions.question: Did the dark urine start during or right after a cold, sore throat or stomach bug?
key_questions.looking_for: Gross hematuria beginning within 1–3 days of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection — the classic synpharyngitic timing

key_questions.question: Has this happened before with other infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes of visible blood in the urine with later infections, with normal-looking urine in between

key_questions.question: Is urinating painful, or do you have to go more often or urgently?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; dysuria, frequency or urgency point to a urinary tract infection instead

key_questions.question: Have you had any fevers, chills or night sweats with this?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; fever with the dark urine suggests infection or a systemic illness

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any swelling in your ankles, feet or around your eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Periorbital or ankle puffiness, which suggests protein loss and a more active glomerular process

key_questions.question: Have you had any rash, especially on the legs or buttocks, or joint pain or swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Palpable purpura or arthritis, which points to IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) or lupus rather than IgA nephropathy

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent sore throat, and was a strep test done?
key_questions.looking_for: A sore throat 1–3 weeks earlier with a positive strep test suggests post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; a cold 1–3 days earlier fits IgA nephropathy

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have high blood pressure or kidney problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Known hypertension or reduced kidney function, which suggests more advanced or progressive disease

key_questions.question: Do you have any conditions such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, cirrhosis or HIV?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions associated with secondary IgA nephropathy

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have kidney disease, blood in the urine, or kidney failure at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of IgA nephropathy, other glomerulonephritis, or hereditary nephritis such as Alport syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had any hearing loss, ringing in the ears or recurrent nosebleeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hearing loss and ocular findings suggest Alport syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had any unintentional weight loss, oral ulcers or sensitivity to sunlight?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these systemic features suggest lupus nephritis

key_questions.question: Have you taken any medications or supplements that could affect the kidneys?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs or nephrotoxic agents that could contribute to kidney injury

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status, which is needed before kidney biopsy or immunosuppressive therapy and helps distinguish preeclampsia

reasoning_points: Episodic gross hematuria beginning within 1–3 days of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (synpharyngitic timing)
Recurrent episodes of dark, cola- or tea-colored urine with normal-appearing urine between episodes
Hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts indicating a glomerular source of bleeding
Proteinuria, hypertension or reduced kidney function suggesting progressive disease
Absence of systemic features such as palpable purpura, arthritis, oral ulcers or rash, which argues against IgA vasculitis and lupus
Normal complement levels (C3 and C4), which favor IgA nephropathy over lupus nephritis or post-infectious glomerulonephritis
Kidney biopsy showing dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, confirming the diagnosis
Exclusion of secondary causes such as cirrhosis, celiac disease and HIV infection

easy: Young adult male with recurrent episodes of cola-colored urine starting 1–2 days after a cold
Gross hematuria with no dysuria, fever or rash
Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts
Normal kidney function and blood pressure between episodes
medium: Persistent microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria found on routine urinalysis
Woman of reproductive age with hematuria and proteinuria, requiring exclusion of lupus nephritis
Patient with hypertension and slowly rising creatinine but no visible blood in the urine
Recent sore throat with hematuria, requiring distinction from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
hard: Older adult with isolated microscopic hematuria and reduced kidney function, requiring workup for secondary causes
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine over days and crescents on biopsy
Child with gross hematuria and abdominal pain, requiring distinction from IgA vasculitis
Patient with cirrhosis or celiac disease and new hematuria, raising the question of secondary IgA nephropathy
Pregnant patient with hematuria and proteinuria mistaken for preeclampsia
